text.tspan: Everyday English - C1 - 2026/10/31 - Grammar - 01

svg.title: Trying a costume on is only the first step; it must also work in motion.

text.tspan: Trying a costume on is only the first step; it must also work in motion.
Inversion after only then
When Only then opens a clause meaning “not until that
moment,” place the auxiliary before the subject.
I tried walking in the full costume. Only then did I realize that
the mask blocked my view.
Past simple: Only then did + subject + base verb. Past perfect:
Only then had + subject + past participle. No inversion in “I
only then realized…”; this fronted pattern is more emphatic.
A: Did the costume work when you tried it on?
B: It looked fine in the mirror. Then I tried going down the
steps.
A: What happened?
B: Only then did I realize I couldn’t see my feet through the
mask.
Rewrite as one sentence beginning Only then: “We tested the
costume in the dark. At that moment, we noticed that the
sleeves covered the reflective strips.” (Model: Only then did we
notice that the sleeves covered the reflective strips. Use
notice, not noticed, after did.)
